name: 16 Grid · Fuel Cell · BESS — Shaped Load 5%→40%→120%→40%→20% (90 min)
description: 90-minute shaped load profile supplied by grid import, fuel cell array, and BESS (grid-tied to PG&E at 50 MW firm; 20 MW / 4-stack fuel cell module array; 6 MW / 8 MWh BESS starting at 85% SoC). No gas turbines, no solar. Load advances through five phases: t=0:00 warm-up floor at ~5% (2 MW); t=10:00 step to 40% (16.1 MW facility); t=30:00 overload burst to 120% (48.3 MW — grid import covers the burst; no import cap is set, so the BESS stays in reserve per DR-2026-10-27-GRID-MODE-BESS); t=50:00 recovery back to 40%; t=60:00 step down to 20% (8.1 MW) and hold to end of run. Use to exercise grid-import metering, fuel cell dispatch, and BESS reserve hold in a clean zero-combustion-turbine configuration. (Deterministic — workload-event driven.)
demo_description:
## What this scenario simulates

A GPU data center on grid power, a fuel cell array and a battery, with no gas turbines and no solar. Load follows the same five-phase shaped profile as the SV1 overload demo, so the two can be compared directly.

The site is grid-tied (50 MW firm, advisory, no import cap set), with a 20 MW fuel cell array (4 × 5 MW stacks) and a 6 MW battery (8 MWh usable, starting at 85% charge).

---

## The five load phases

**Phase 1 — Warm-up (t = 0:00 – 10:00, ~2 MW)**
146 GPU nodes at a quiet floor. Fuel cell and grid cover the site; the battery holds charge.

**Phase 2 — Normal operations (t = 10:00 – 30:00, ~16 MW)**
Node count rises to 1,169. The fuel cell array carries most of the load, with grid import making up the rest.

**Phase 3 — Overload burst ⚠️ (t = 30:00 – 50:00, ~48 MW)**
Node count surges to 3,508. The fuel cell array ramps toward its 20 MW ceiling and grid import carries the remainder. With no import cap, the battery does **not** discharge; it holds its 85% charge in reserve (DR-2026-10-27-GRID-MODE-BESS, D1).

**Phase 4 — Recovery (t = 50:00 – 60:00, ~16 MW)**
Load steps back to 40%; grid import falls back.

**Phase 5 — Low-load coast (t = 60:00 – 90:00, ~8 MW)**
585 nodes remain. Watch how fuel cell output settles against grid import.

---

## What the scheduler layer shows

While the physics engine drives the power curves above, the Compute Racks panel shows the actual job traffic that would be causing this load profile in a real facility:

- **Tenant A (Slurm)** submits HPC batch jobs using the slurmrestd wire format — the same JSON a real Slurm cluster would send to GridSignal. Each job shows the node range it occupies, GPU resource strings, and its current queue state.
- **Tenant B (Kubernetes)** submits GPU training workloads as `batch/v1` Job manifests — the format Kubernetes itself uses when you inspect a running job.
- **Tenant C (Ray)** submits distributed training and inference deployments as WorkloadSignal events — each carrying a unique ULID, a hardware profile ID, and the live event type (queued → starting → running → job_end).

Jobs arrive in bursts roughly every 2–5 minutes throughout the run, with individual jobs lasting 1–5 minutes. During the overload phase you will see the queues fill faster than jobs complete — exactly the condition that causes the power spike.

---

## What to watch as an operator

1. **Grid import meter** — peaks during Phase 3; it is the main source above fuel cell output.
2. **Fuel cell output** — watch it ramp toward 20 MW at t = 30:00 and throttle back afterwards.
3. **Battery SoC bar** — should hold at 85% for the whole run. A drop would be a regression against D1.
4. **Tenant MW bars** — each tenant's bar should stay below its contracted ceiling.

## What to watch as an investor

The same 120% spike as the turbine-based demo, served with zero combustion turbines and no unserved load. The grid and fuel cells carry the burst, and the battery stays in reserve. Compare peak grid import and fuel cell utilisation against demo 15.
